content: Dietary patterns, specific foods, nutrients, and other dietary components are intricately linked to the risk of developing various types of cancer. Although precise quantitative estimates of these risks are not yet available, it has been suggested that dietary factors may contribute to approximately 35% of cancer-related deaths. There is growing evidence that diets rich in fiber-containing foods are associated with a lower risk of cancer, particularly colorectal cancer. Additionally, some studies have indicated that diets abundant in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains may reduce the risk of cancers affecting the breast, rectum, oral cavity, pharynx, stomach, and other sites. Carotenoids, which are found in certain fruits and vegetables, have been shown to reduce the risk of several cancers, with particularly strong evidence for lung cancer, even when smoking is accounted for as a confounding factor. Vitamin C, present in citrus fruits, green vegetables, and fortified foods, has also been studied extensively. Among epidemiological studies examining the role of vitamin C, three-quarters have demonstrated that vitamin C or vitamin C-rich fruits provide significant protective effects against cancer. However, more recent research has questioned the protective role of dietary fiber in reducing the risk of colorectal cancer. For example, a major study conducted in 2002 concluded that a low-fat, high-fiber diet rich in fruits and vegetables did not influence prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels in men over a four-year period and did not reduce the incidence of prostate cancer. The earlier belief that dietary fiber prevents certain cancers was largely based on epidemiological observations of low cancer incidence in developing countries. Dr. Denis Burkitt, a prominent advocate of this theory, popularized it in his 1979 book, Don't Forget Fibre in Your Diet. Interestingly, he also proposed that the squatting posture used for defecation in developing countries might play a role in preventing colon diseases. As the fiber hypothesis has faced challenges in replication, his theory regarding defecation posture has gained attention as a potential area for further research. Methionine metabolism has emerged as a critical area of investigation in cancer biology. Methionine, an essential amino acid obtained through dietary intake of proteins (e.g., meat) or methyl donors (e.g., choline and betaine found in beef, eggs, and certain vegetables), plays a central role in cellular processes. Methionine is converted into S-adenosyl methionine (SAM), a key metabolite involved in polyamine synthesis (e.g., spermidine) and cysteine formation. Methionine breakdown products are recycled back into methionine through homocysteine remethylation and methylthioadenosine (MTA) conversion. Vitamins B6, B12, folic acid, and choline are essential cofactors in these reactions. SAM serves as a substrate for methylation reactions catalyzed by DNA, RNA, and protein methyltransferases, producing methylated DNA, RNA, or proteins, along with S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH). SAH acts as a feedback inhibitor of methyltransferase enzymes, and the SAM:SAH ratio directly regulates cellular methylation. Levels of vitamins B6, B12, folic acid, and choline indirectly influence methylation through their roles in the methionine metabolism cycle. A hallmark of cancer is the dysregulation of the methionine metabolic pathway, often resulting in reduced levels of SAM and/or SAM-dependent methylation. This maladaptation can arise from genetic or environmental factors. For example, deficiencies in enzymes such as methylthioadenosine phosphorylase, methionine dependency in cancer cells, elevated polyamine synthesis, or diets lacking methyl donors or containing methylation inhibitors have all been linked to tumor formation. Studies in mice, rats, and humans have consistently shown a strong correlation between reduced SAM levels and cancer development. While many theories have been proposed regarding the role of DNA methylation and its impact on DNA mutation and repair, the discovery that methyltransferases influenced by SAM levels also function as tumor suppressors provides a more direct connection. This finding has significant implications for both chemoprevention and chemotherapy strategies. Protein arginine N-methyltransferase-4 (PRMT4) plays a pivotal role in transcriptional regulation by methylating arginine residues within proteins. PRMT4 interacts with transcriptional activators such as p160 and CBP/p300, modifying these proteins to enhance gene expression via steroid hormone receptors. Notably, PRMT4 also methylates core histones H3 and H4, which are targets of the histone acetylase activity of CBP/p300 coactivators. By recruiting PRMT4 to chromatin through coactivator binding, histone methylation is increased, thereby improving the accessibility of promoter regions for transcription. Additionally, PRMT4-mediated methylation of the transcriptional coactivator CBP inhibits its binding to CREB, effectively reallocating the limited cellular pool of CBP for interactions with steroid hormone receptors.
